nameStory: The name 'cursed crowfoot' comes from this plant's notorious reputation for causing severe skin burns and blisters when handled. The 'crowfoot' part refers to the deeply divided leaves that supposedly resemble a crow's foot, a name shared by many buttercup relatives. Medieval herbalists considered it so dangerously toxic that they literally cursed its existence!
description: Cursed crowfoot is a smooth, hairless annual plant that grows 1-2 feet tall in wet places throughout New England. It's a member of the buttercup family but looks quite different from the cheerful meadow buttercups most people know. This plant has small, pale yellow flowers and distinctive deeply-cut leaves that give it an almost celery-like appearance. Despite its delicate looks, it's one of the most toxic plants in our region.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Lower leaves are deeply divided into three main segments that are further cut into narrow, celery-like lobes. They feel smooth and slightly succulent to the touch, with a glossy appearance that catches the light.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny pale yellow flowers, only about 1/4 inch across, with 5 petals that are shorter than the sepals underneath. The petals are so small they almost look like they're missing compared to other buttercups.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Grows as a smooth, branching annual plant that's completely hairless throughout. The stems are hollow, thick, and often have a reddish tinge, especially near the base.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Produces distinctive cylindrical clusters of tiny, wrinkled seeds that look like miniature corn cobs. These seed heads are much longer than they are wide, unlike most other buttercups.

idTips.label: Habitat Clue
idTips.description: Always found in or right next to water - muddy pond edges, stream banks, or wet ditches. The plant often has its roots actually in standing water.

habitat: Look for cursed crowfoot in wet, muddy places throughout New England - pond edges, stream banks, roadside ditches, and marshy areas. It thrives in disturbed wet soils and often grows right at the water's edge where its roots can stay constantly moist. You'll typically find it mixed with other wetland plants like sedges, rushes, and watercress.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge early with their characteristic celery-like leaves. Small pale yellow flowers begin blooming in late spring and continue through summer.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming period with tiny flowers and developing seed heads. The distinctive corn cob-like seed clusters become most obvious during this season.
seasonality.fall: Plants begin to die back as an annual, leaving behind mature seeds. The cylindrical seed heads may persist briefly before dispersing.
seasonality.winter: No above-ground parts remain as this is an annual plant. Seeds overwinter in the mud and will germinate the following spring.

funFact: This innocent-looking plant contains such powerful toxins that just brushing against it can cause severe chemical burns that don't appear for hours - earning it the nickname 'blister buttercup' and making it more dangerous to touch than poison ivy!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with celery or water parsley due to its deeply-cut leaves, but remember the simple rule: if it has yellow buttercup flowers, don't touch it! The tiny pale yellow petals are the dead giveaway that this is the dangerous cursed crowfoot, not an edible herb.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'cursed crowfoot,' this plant is also known as 'celery-leaved buttercup' because of its leaf shape - but never confuse it with actual celery! This naming similarity has unfortunately led to accidental poisonings when foragers mistake the leaves for edible wild celery or water parsley.
compareHints: Unlike other New England buttercups that have bright, showy yellow flowers, cursed crowfoot has tiny, pale, almost insignificant blooms. Its smooth, succulent-like stems and water-loving habitat also set it apart from meadow-dwelling relatives like creeping buttercup or bulbous buttercup. The corn cob-shaped seed clusters are unique among our local buttercups and provide a foolproof identification feature.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's buttercups, small-flowered buttercup is unmistakable due to its tiny petals - all other buttercup species have much more prominent yellow flowers.
Among New England's buttercups, hooked buttercup is unique for its woodland habitat and tiny, pale flowers—most other buttercups prefer sunny, open areas and have much brighter, larger yellow blooms.
Among New England's many buttercup species, meadow buttercup stands out for its tall, upright growth and deeply palm-divided leaves.
Unlike meadow buttercup which grows in upright clumps, or bulbous buttercup with its swollen stem base, creeping buttercup is the only common buttercup that spreads by runners along the ground.
Among New England's many buttercup species, bulbous buttercup is the only one with that distinctive swollen stem base.
Among New England buttercups, bristly crowfoot stands out for its rough, hairy texture and pale flowers - most other buttercups have smoother leaves and bright golden-yellow blooms.
Among New England's many buttercups, yellow water-crowfoot is one of the few truly aquatic species, distinguished by its floating stems and dramatic leaf differences between air and water.
Among New England's buttercups, creeping spearwort is unique for its simple, narrow leaves - all other local buttercups have divided or lobed leaves.
Unlike the robust meadow buttercup or creeping buttercup with their typical three-lobed leaves, fen crowfoot has leaves so finely divided they look almost thread-like.

Among New England's many buttercups, early buttercup stands out for its combination of very early bloom time, preference for dry rather than moist habitats, and distinctively narrow, deeply-cut leaves.
Unlike the common meadow buttercup which grows tall and robust in fields, Allegheny Mountain buttercup stays much smaller and more delicate.
Rock buttercup stands out from other New England buttercups by having the smallest, palest flowers in the family - most other buttercups have bright golden-yellow blooms.
Among the 20+ buttercup species in New England, lesser spearwort stands out immediately because of its narrow, spear-shaped leaves – all other buttercups have lobed, divided, or rounded leaves.
Unlike the common meadow buttercup which prefers drier ground and grows much taller, swamp buttercup stays low and spreads along wet soil.
Among New England's aquatic buttercups, longbeak buttercup is distinguished by its exceptionally long fruit beaks and preference for flowing water.

Among New England's many buttercups, bristly buttercup stands out primarily for its rough, hairy texture - most other species like meadow buttercup and creeping buttercup have relatively smooth stems and leaves.

Unlike terrestrial buttercups like meadow buttercup or creeping buttercup, small yellow water-crowfoot is adapted for aquatic life with thicker, more succulent leaves and a strictly prostrate growth habit.
Unlike all other New England buttercups that grow upright, Lapland buttercup stays completely flat and creeping.
Among New England's many buttercups, water-plantain spearwort is unique for its completely undivided, lance-shaped leaves - most other buttercups have deeply lobed or divided leaves.
Unlike its terrestrial buttercup cousins that have typical yellow flowers, thread-leaved water-crowfoot has white petals with yellow centers and specialized underwater foliage.
